messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

David, a nineteen-year-old UX designer with a keen eye for clean interfaces and intuitive user flow, had always found a sense of order and predictability in the digital world. His life in the city was structured around his work at a small tech startup, his evening coding classes, and a tight-knit group of friends he’d known since high school. That sense of predictable safety began to unravel six months ago. It started online, with an anonymous profile on a design forum that was unusually complimentary of his work, then persistently inquisitive about his personal life. David, accustomed to online networking, was polite but firm with his boundaries. The messages escalated, becoming obsessive and then threatening. Two weeks later, a typed note appeared on the windshield of his car, parked outside his apartment, referencing a specific detail from one of their private online conversations. The world suddenly felt porous and unsafe. The anonymous person knew where he lived.

The next month was a blur of fear. He would see a figure in a grey hoodie standing across the street from his office building, only to have them melt into the crowd when he looked again. He started taking different routes home, his keys clutched in his fist. The breaking point came when he returned to his apartment to find a single, long-stemmed white rose left on his doormat, identical to one visible in a photo on his long-deleted personal blog. He called the police, but with no clear suspect and no overt physical threat, there was little they could do. He broke his lease the next day, moving to a new apartment in a different part of the city and telling no one but his immediate family his new address. He switched to working fully remotely, his manager agreeing that the stress was impacting his focus at the office.

David holds a set of core convictions about the world. He is certain that it is a fundamentally dangerous place. A deep-seated belief he carries is that he must be exceptionally careful, that constant vigilance is the only rational response to the unseen threats that could emerge at any moment. He also believes, with a quiet and unshakable certainty, that what happened was his own fault, a direct consequence of the way he acted. He replays his initial online interactions, convinced that his friendly tone was an invitation, that sharing any detail about his life was a catastrophic error in judgment.

He has systematically tried to erase his digital footprint, a difficult task for someone in his profession. He has deleted all personal social media, and his professional portfolio is now password-protected. His friendships have become strained; he rarely initiates contact and often declines invitations, unwilling to explain the gnawing preoccupation that makes socialising feel like an impossible performance of normalcy. The clean, logical world of user interface design, once a source of pleasure, now feels like a hollow echo of a control he no longer possesses. The logic of code and design principles cannot protect him from the illogical nature of human threat. He came to therapy after his mother, during a rare visit, found him sitting in his darkened apartment, having not left for three days. He told her he felt trapped, not by a person anymore, but by a feeling. He hopes, he said in his first session, to learn how to exist in the world again without feeling like he is constantly waiting for the other shoe to drop.
